query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Elevated-temperature exposure in oxidizing or reducing gases degrades the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA by a mechanism in which the formation and stability of an externally grown, compositionally selective protective oxide scale (rich in Al and Ti) controls the degradation rate. Under oxidizing atmospheres, the protective oxide forms but gradually accumulates internal stresses due to growth mismatches and thermal expansion differences with the FCC matrix, eventually leading to scale spallation and localized stress concentrations that promote rapid mechanical failure. Under reducing conditions, the lack of a coherent, externally protective scale allows more pervasive internal oxidation and void formation along grain boundaries, also compromising load-bearing capability and leading to catastrophic failure.
generation.material_initial_state: An additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with a stable FCC matrix and a fine, homogeneous distribution of precipitates, free of significant oxide layers or internal voids.
generation.intervention: Expose samples to controlled gas environments that vary in oxygen partial pressure (from oxidizing to reducing conditions) at elevated temperatures (e.g., above 800°C) while holding other thermal parameters constant.
generation.conditions: High-temperature exposure (≥800°C) with well-controlled gas atmospheres differing in oxygen potential, ranging from oxygen-rich (oxidizing) to oxygen-poor (reducing).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and evolution of an oxide scale at the surface and grain boundaries, whose integrity (or failure by spallation) mediates local stress concentrations and subsequent microstructural degradation.
generation.mechanism: In oxidizing environments, initial formation of a coherent, protective Al/Ti-rich oxide scale temporarily slows degradation; however, continued oxidation leads to growth-induced internal stresses and eventual spallation, exposing fresh high-entropy alloy to rapid oxidation. In reducing environments, the diminished external oxide scale allows oxygen to penetrate and oxidize internally at grain boundaries, leading to void formation and enhanced creep, which together precipitate catastrophic failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the starting baseline with no oxide scale or internal voids, samples exposed to oxidizing conditions will show an initially protective oxide layer that eventually spalls, leading to rapid deterioration of mechanical properties, while samples in reducing environments will exhibit more uniform internal oxidation and void formation with gradual yet significant degradation in creep resistance and tensile strength.
generation.baseline: The as-fabricated state characterized by an intact FCC matrix with fine precipitates, free from significant oxide scales or internal oxidation damage.
generation.boundary: This behavior is expected under high-temperature exposures (≥800°C) with controlled oxygen partial pressures; effects may differ if temperatures or gas compositions fall outside these high-temperature, high oxygen-potential regimes.
generation.uncertainty: The exact composition, adherence, and growth kinetics of the oxide scale, as well as the relative contributions of creep versus oxidation-induced damage, remain uncertain and could vary with slight modifications in alloy chemistry or processing history.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical alloy samples and subject them to two sets of controlled high-temperature tests (≥800°C): one set under an oxidizing atmosphere and the other under a reducing atmosphere. Monitor the samples in situ using high-resolution microscopy and stress measurement techniques. After exposure, perform detailed microstructural and compositional analyses (e.g., SEM, TEM, EDS/XPS) of surface oxide scales, grain boundaries, and measure mechanical properties (tensile and creep tests).
measurements: Thickness, composition, and adherence of the oxide scale (via SEM, TEM, and XPS)
Residual stress analysis in the oxide layer and underlying matrix (using X-ray diffraction or similar techniques)
Mechanical property evaluation (tensile yield strength, creep resistance)
Internal microstructural changes (void formation and grain boundary oxidation via high-resolution imaging)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If oxidizing environments do not exhibit evidence of a protective oxide scale that undergoes spallation correlating with abrupt mechanical degradation, or if reducing environments do not show significant internal oxidation and void formation leading to degradation, then the hypothesis that protective oxide formation and its failure governs degradation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
The High Temperature Tensile and Creep Behaviors of High Entropy Superalloy

Abstract: AbstractThis article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L12 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior.
